steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our networking paper proposing a framework where reinforcement learning agents dynamically tune the parameters of traditional congestion control protocols in data centers, with BBR as the case study. Explain why congestion control is hard, why pure online learning falls short, how our framework works, and summarize the headline results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Congestion control and why it is hard
- Diverse, changing network environments
- Experts vs. online learning approaches
- Our idea: RL tunes traditional protocols on a slower time scale
- Framework workflow
- Case study: BBR and its parameters
- Implementation and results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Congestion control
  - crucial in networking: divides limited shared resources (link bandwidth, buffers, etc) among flows
  - very challenging: high total utilization, fair to individual flows, avoid congestion, distributed
  - decades of research, many protocols; none meets requirements of all networks
- Environments
  - vary in latency, volatility, buffer capacity, other dimensions -> engineer protocol per environment or suboptimal
  - dynamic traffic: number of flows, burstiness, application types change -> statically-tuned parameters no longer optimal
- Experts vs online learning
  - designers = experts at rules for adjusting rates; can't expect them to modify rules dynamically
  - online learning solutions (cite): recent attention, promise to generalize protocols, no per-environment engineering
  - promise not realized in practice: control loops very small, esp. data centers (cite) -> accurate agent action hard
- Our idea
  - high-level changes orders of magnitude less frequent than control loops
  - leverage expert-designed protocols; machines adjust them on scale of seconds to hours
  - framework for dynamically adjusting congestion control parameters in data center
  - microsecond-scale actions: traditional protocols; higher-level loop: RL agents set key parameters
- Workflow
  - operator specifies variant, parameters to adjust, requirements as reward function
  - end-hosts send network/traffic state to online learning module via communication channel
  - module: multi-agent RL, periodically outputs tuned parameters
- BBR case study
  - bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip propagation time (BBR) (cite) as base variant
  - promising in Google's environment; migrating elsewhere may degrade, huge readjustment effort
  - tune two parameters: RTT minimum filter window, bottleneck bandwidth maximum filter window
- Results
  - implemented, prototype tested for BBR; design generic, extendable to other protocols
  - frequent changes: BBR estimates RTT accurately 40\% of time; ours >60\% of testing time
  - multiple flows: convergence time of BBR reduced 2.7 x, peak RTT reduced 40\%

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Congestion control is a crucial part of computer networking. It decides how limited shared resources (link bandwidth, buffers, etc) are divided between different network flows. The problem is very challenging, because it has to keep the total resource utilization high, serve individual flows fairly, and avoid congestion, all in a distributed way. There have been decades of research and a large number of protocols have been developed, but no congestion control protocol can meet the requirements of all networks.

Network environments are very different in latency, volatility, buffer capacity, and many other dimensions. This means a congestion control protocol has to be engineered specifically for an environment, or else it will not perform optimally in that environment. Also, traffic patterns behave dynamically, which makes the problem even harder, since the number of flows, the traffic burstiness, and the types of applications change over time, and so the optimal values of statically-tuned parameters stop being valid.

Congestion control designers are experts in understanding the congestion control problem and in defining rules for adjusting rates in a network environment. But we cannot expect an expert to change the rules dynamically when the network changes. To address these problems, online learning solutions have recently been getting attention, with the promise of generalizing congestion control protocols so that they do not need to be engineered for every environment. In practice, though, this promise has not been realized. The main problem is that congestion control loops are very small, especially in data centers, which makes it difficult for an artificial agent to take an accurate control action.

High-level changes in a network environment happen orders of magnitude less often than congestion control loops. So we can use the pre-knowledge in congestion control protocols designed by experts, and use machines to adjust them dynamically on time scales of seconds to hours. In this paper we propose a framework that dynamically adjusts congestion control parameters in a data center. We use traditional protocols for the congestion control actions, which happen on the order of microseconds in a data center. In a higher-level control loop, we use Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents to decide the values of key parameters of the traditional protocols.

- Workflow
  - operator specifies variant, parameters to adjust, requirements as reward function
  - end-hosts send network/traffic state to online learning module via communication channel
  - module: multi-agent RL, periodically outputs tuned parameters
- BBR case study
  - BBR (cite) as base variant; promising in Google's environment, migration may degrade, huge readjustment effort
  - tune RTT minimum filter window, bottleneck bandwidth maximum filter window
- Results
  - prototype for BBR; generic design, extendable
  - frequent changes: BBR 40\% accurate RTT estimation vs ours >60\%
  - multiple flows: convergence time 2.7 x lower, peak RTT 40\% lower

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Congestion control is a crucial part of computer networking. It decides how limited shared resources (link bandwidth, buffers, etc) are divided between different network flows. The problem is very challenging, because it has to keep the total resource utilization high, serve individual flows fairly, and avoid congestion, all in a distributed way. There have been decades of research and a large number of protocols have been developed, but no congestion control protocol can meet the requirements of all networks.

Network environments are very different in latency, volatility, buffer capacity, and many other dimensions. This means a congestion control protocol has to be engineered specifically for an environment, or else it will not perform optimally in that environment. Also, traffic patterns behave dynamically, which makes the problem even harder, since the number of flows, the traffic burstiness, and the types of applications change over time, and so the optimal values of statically-tuned parameters stop being valid.

Congestion control designers are experts in understanding the congestion control problem and in defining rules for adjusting rates in a network environment. But we cannot expect an expert to change the rules dynamically when the network changes. To address these problems, online learning solutions have recently been getting attention, with the promise of generalizing congestion control protocols so that they do not need to be engineered for every environment. In practice, though, this promise has not been realized. The main problem is that congestion control loops are very small, especially in data centers, which makes it difficult for an artificial agent to take an accurate control action.

High-level changes in a network environment happen orders of magnitude less often than congestion control loops. So we can use the pre-knowledge in congestion control protocols designed by experts, and use machines to adjust them dynamically on time scales of seconds to hours. In this paper we propose a framework that dynamically adjusts congestion control parameters in a data center. We use traditional protocols for the congestion control actions, which happen on the order of microseconds in a data center. In a higher-level control loop, we use Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents to decide the values of key parameters of the traditional protocols.

In more detail, the network operator specifies the congestion control variant, the parameters that should be adjusted dynamically, and the network requirements as a reward function. The end-hosts send the network and traffic state to the online learning module we designed through a communication channel. The online learning module is a multi-agent reinforcement learning solution, and it periodically generates the tuned congestion control parameters.

As a case study, we use bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip propagation time (BBR) as the base congestion control variant. BBR shows promising performance in Google's environment, but moving BBR to other environments might make its performance worse, and a huge effort is needed to readjust the parameters. Using our framework, we dynamically tune two of BBR's parameters that we think have a big effect on its behavior, the RTT minimum filter window and the bottleneck bandwidth maximum filter window.

We implemented the framework and tested a prototype specifically for BBR. The design and implementation of the framework are generic, and the evaluation can be extended to other congestion control protocols. For a network with frequent changes, BBR can only estimate the RTT accurately 40\% of the time, while our RL-based framework gives a correct estimation for more than 60\% of the testing time. Also, in a scenario with multiple flows, it reduces the convergence time of BBR by 2.7 x and the peak RTT by 40\%.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Congestion control is a crucial component in computer networking, determining how limited shared resources (link bandwidth, buffers, etc) are divided among different network flows. The problem is extremely challenging, as it should keep total resource utilization high while fairly serving individual flows and avoiding congestion in a distributed manner. Despite decades of research and the development of a large number of protocols, no congestion control protocol can meet the requirements of all networks.

Network environments vary significantly in latency, volatility, buffer capacity, and many other dimensions, which means that a congestion control protocol must either be engineered specifically for an environment or fail to perform optimally in it. The dynamic behavior of traffic patterns further complicates the problem: the number of flows, traffic burstiness, and types of applications change over time, invalidating the optimal values of statically-tuned parameters.

Congestion control designers are experts in understanding the congestion control problem and in defining rules for adjusting rates in a network environment, but we cannot expect an expert to modify the rules dynamically as the network changes. To address these problems, online learning solutions [1,2,3] have recently been getting attention, promising to generalize congestion control protocols and remove the need to engineer them for every environment. In practice, however, this promise is not realized. The main problem is that congestion control loops are very small, especially in data centers [4], which makes accurate control actions by an artificial agent difficult.

High-level changes in a network environment happen orders of magnitude less frequently than congestion control loops. We can therefore leverage the pre-knowledge of congestion control protocols designed by experts and use machines to adjust them dynamically on time scales of seconds to hours. In this paper, we propose a framework for dynamically adjusting congestion control parameters in a data center. For congestion control actions, which happen on the order of microseconds in a data center, we use traditional protocols; in a higher-level control loop, Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents determine the values of key parameters of these protocols.

More specifically, the network operator specifies the congestion control variant, the parameters to be adjusted dynamically, and the network requirements in terms of a reward function. The end-hosts send the network and traffic state through a communication channel to the online learning module we designed, which consists of a multi-agent reinforcement learning solution and periodically generates the tuned congestion control parameters.

As a case study, we consider bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip propagation time (BBR) [5] as our base congestion control variant. BBR shows promising results in Google's environment; however, migrating it to other environments might degrade its performance and require a huge effort to readjust the parameters. Using our framework, we dynamically tune two of BBR's parameters that we believe greatly affect its behavior: the RTT minimum filter window and the bottleneck bandwidth maximum filter window.

We implement the proposed framework and test a prototype specifically for BBR, although its design and implementation are generic and the evaluation can be extended to other congestion control protocols. In a network with frequent changes, BBR accurately estimates the RTT only 40\% of the time, whereas our RL-based framework provides a correct estimation for more than 60\% of the testing time. Moreover, in a scenario with multiple flows, it reduces the convergence time of BBR by 2.7 x and the peak RTT by 40\%.

References:
[1] N. Jay, N. Rotman, B. Godfrey, M. Schapira, and A. Tamar, “A deep reinforcement learning perspective on Internet congestion control,” in Proceedings of the International Conference on Machine Learning , 2019, pp. 3050–3059.
[2] S. Emara, B. Li, and Y. Chen, “Eagle: Refining congestion control by learning from the experts,” in Proceedings of the IEEE INFOCOM - IEEE Conference on Computer Communications , 2020, pp. 676–685.
[3] M. Dong, T. Meng, D. Zarchy, E. Arslan, Y. Gilad, P. B. Godfrey, and M. Schapira, “PCC Vivace: Online-learning congestion control,” in Proceedings of the 15th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation , 2018, pp. 343–356.
[4] H. Dong, A. Munir, H. Tout, and Y. Ganjali, “Next-generation data center network enabled by machine learning: Review, challenges, and opportunities,” IEEE Access , vol. 9, pp. 136 459–136 475, 2021.
[5] N. Cardwell, Y. Cheng, C. S. Gunn, S. H. Yeganeh, and V. Jacobson, “BBR: Congestion-based congestion control,” Queue , vol. 14, no. 5, pp. 20–53, 2016.
